stories.headline: Nepal floods spotlight westward GLOF threat in Ladakh, Chenab Valley, Kashmir
stories.title: Nepal floods spotlight westward GLOF threat in Ladakh, Chenab Valley, Kashmir
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 27: A deadly glacial collapse and debris flow along the Nepal-Tibet border has renewed concern over risks from retreating glaciers and changing high-altitude catchments across the Himalaya, including Ladakh and the Chenab Valley in Jammu and Kashmir. The August 26 disaster sent water, ice, mud, and debris through valleys in Nepal and Tibet, killing more than 180 people and leaving more than 1300 missing, according to preliminary reports. Roads, bridges, and settlements were damaged or destroyed. The US Geological Survey said seismic activity initially interpreted as an earthquake was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow that caused catastrophic downstream impacts. The Nepal disaster comes as a new study warns that climate change could shift Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazards westward, from the eastern Himalaya toward the central and western Himalaya, including Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. Western Himalaya emerges as climate hotspot Researchers from Birla Institute of Technology (BIT), Mesra, the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, and Ashoka University analysed 120 years of temperature and snow-cover changes along with climate projections. The research, 'Vulnerability of the Himalayan region under climate change,' was published online June 9, 2026, in the Journal of Earth System Science. It identifies the western Himalaya - covering Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh - as the most climate-sensitive of the three Himalayan sectors examined. The study lead by Protyusha Mukhopadhyay of the Department of Remote Sensing and Geoinformatics, BIT Mesra; also included T P Sabin of the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology; Swagata Payra and Akhouri Pramod Krishna of BIT Mesra; and Parthasarathi Mukhopadhyay of Ashoka University. "The east has become a hotspot for glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs)," the study said. "That risk is expected to spread westward in the future, driven by retreating glaciers and the new lakes they leave behind, not by temperature alone," it said. The western Himalaya has warmed by about 1 degree Celsius since the early 20th century, the study found. Under a high-emissions pathway, winter temperatures during 2081-2100 could rise 7.18 degrees Celsius above early-20th-century levels in the western Himalaya. The projected rise is 6.71 degrees in the central Himalaya and 5.82 degrees in the eastern Himalaya. The western Himalaya is also projected to experience the sharpest snow loss, with implications for glacier retreat, meltwater flows and downstream water availability. "The western Himalaya consistently emerges as the most sensitive stretch - it warms the most and loses the most snow under every pathway we tested," the study said. "In the west and centre, winters are warming faster than springs," it said. "Less snow on the ground would mean a darker surface, which absorbs more heat, which melts more snow," the study said. Nighttime temperatures are also rising faster than daytime temperatures across the western and central Himalaya, potentially altering the timing and pace of snowmelt, the study found. The researchers called for sustained monitoring of glaciers and glacial lakes, stronger ground observations and improved early-warning systems. Ladakh, Chenab Valley face greater concern Climate scientist Prof Ghulam Jeelani, dean of the School of Earth and Environmental Sciences at the University of Kashmir, said the immediate GLOF concern in Jammu and Kashmir is higher in Ladakh and the Chenab Valley than in the Kashmir Valley. "Zanskar, Nubra and Shyok are particularly vulnerable because glaciers are retreating rapidly and new glacial lakes are forming," Dr Jeelani told Greater Kashmir. "These lakes originate due to glacial recession. Most are moraine-dammed lakes, formed behind loose glacial debris, and such lakes are inherently more vulnerable to outburst floods," he said. Dr Jeelani said glacier-fed upper catchments in Chenab valley - Kishtwar, Doda and Ramban also warrant scrutiny because a breach upstream could send floodwaters rapidly through narrow valleys. The wider western Himalayan belt, including Himachal Pradesh, also requires closer monitoring as glaciers retreat and snow patterns change. But Dr Jeelani cautioned against treating the presence or expansion of a glacial lake as evidence of imminent GLOFs. "In Kashmir, many of these lakes have existed for centuries and have never burst. Their stability cannot be judged only through satellite imagery," he said. "Remote sensing can identify lakes and monitor their expansion, but it cannot determine the geological stability of a moraine dam. That requires detailed field investigations," Dr Jeelani said. He said potentially hazardous lakes should be assessed through field investigations, while downstream exposure, monitoring and early-warning systems should be strengthened.

stories.headline: UP sounds high alert in border districts after deadly Nepal floods
stories.title: UP sounds high alert in border districts after deadly Nepal floods
stories.summary: UP sounds high alert in border districts after deadly Nepal floods
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Uttar Pradesh has sounded a high alert in border districts and sent rescue teams to Nepal after deadly flash floods.
The move comes as river levels rise, Indian tourists remain missing and vulnerable villages are being warned.

The administration has sounded a high alert in Maharajganj and Kushinagar districts of Uttar Pradesh and stepped up monitoring of the Gandak and other water bodies downstream of rivers in Nepal, following devastating flash floods in the neighbouring country that have killed at least 177 people and left thousands missing.
The administration in UP, which shares its northern borders with Nepal, is focusing on river monitoring, alerting vulnerable villages and keeping relief-and-rescue teams ready.

The UP government has deployed a 32-member SDRF platoon and 22 PAC personnel to Nepal for rescue and relief operations following directions from Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, an official statement said.
Four rubber boats are available and an aluminium boat is also being sent with an additional SDRF platoon.
The relief commissioner's control room is monitoring border districts, while families of stranded UP residents can contact the 1070 helpline, it said.
The Nepal floods were triggered after an ice-rock landslide blocked a river near the country's border with China.
The floods have affected several districts and left at least 826 people missing, according to Nepal's disaster management authorities.
Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has said nearly 300 Indian tourists are among those reported missing.
The flash floods have caused extensive damage to bridges and roads, with several major highways blocked.
In Maharajganj, District Magistrate Gaurav Singh Sogarwal and Superintendent of Police Shakti Mohan Avasthy inspected the Narayani river and adjoining areas and reviewed flood preparedness.

article_sentences: The decisions were among eight points of consensus reached during the 25th round of talks between National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on August 25, according to China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The two sides also agreed to hold the next round of the Special Representatives talks in India in 2027.
Under the agreement, two additional meeting points will be created for General Level Mechanism/Senior Highest Military Commander meetings.
India and China will also establish two additional military hotline channels in the eastern and middle sectors of the border.

The two sides agreed that situations on the ground would be handled promptly through existing diplomatic and military channels, including the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination, local commander-level meetings, and other agreed mechanisms.
The aim is to resolve outstanding issues and prevent "misunderstanding and miscalculation" along the Line of Actual Control.
The two sides reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border and creating conditions for the steady development of bilateral ties.

They also agreed to advance negotiations for a framework to settle the boundary dispute based on the 2005 Agreement on Political Parameters and Guiding Principles and subsequent consensus reached during Special Representatives talks.

"The Expert Group on Boundary Delimitation and Working Group on Border Management under the WMCC would respectively advance discussions on an Early and Substantial Harvest of boundary delimitation and Border Management," the Chinese side said, adding that the first task for both these groups would be to agree on their respective Terms of Reference.
India and China also noted progress in trans-border cooperation.
The Indian side appreciated China's efforts to increase the number of batches of Indian pilgrims allowed to visit Mount Gang Renpoche and Lake Mapam Yun Tso in China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
Both sides welcomed the reopening of three designated border trading points and agreed to strengthen cooperation in border trade, pilgrimage, and other areas.

stories.headline: The US Air Force Bomber Fleet Has Shrunk From 500 To 140 Jets As Demand Hits Record Highs
stories.title: The US Air Force Bomber Fleet Has Shrunk From 500 To 140 Jets As Demand Hits Record Highs
stories.summary: The US Air Force has far fewer bombers than it did at the end of the Cold War, but these aircraft are being deployed more frequently around the world.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A Bomber Task Force (BTF) is a deployment of United States Air Force (USAF) bomber aircraft and supporting personnel that allows the Department of War to demonstrate its ability to command and control bomber forces anywhere in the world, on short notice if required.
The first BTF mission took place in 2018 and was undertaken by the 23rd Expeditionary Bomb Squadron.

These missions not only rapidly move heavy, lethal strike capacity to forward areas of the world on short notice, but also provide deterrence, training opportunities with partner nations, and on-call firepower unmatched by lighter aircraft.
BTFs demonstrate resolve and a willingness to use force if necessary.
At issue, however, is the fact that these deployments have continued with increasing regularity despite the USAF's bomber fleet having declined significantly since the conclusion of the Cold War.
From hundreds of bombers at the turn of the millennium to just over 100 airframes today, an increasingly small fleet is answering the ever-growing demand for BTFs around the world.
This has, in turn, led to the need for extensive modernization of the USAF's bomber fleet while the clock ticks toward the arrival of its sixth-generation bomber.
During the Cold War, the USAF's Strategic Air Command was first and foremost tasked with conducting an all-out nuclear retaliation in the event of a nuclear confrontation with the Soviet Union.

This mission required immense global infrastructure and a massive bomber fleet to ensure not only deterrence, but also the ability to conduct immediate, wide-ranging, and crippling attacks against Soviet military sites and industrial capacity.
As this nearly 45-year competition ended in 1991, the USAF maintained a fleet of more than 500 bombers.
Fast-forward 35 years, and that once-massive bomber fleet has dramatically diminished to a force of around 140 aircraft.

The reasoning was obvious and practical: the existential threat to the US and Western Europe had essentially disappeared, and there was no longer a perceived need to maintain such a large bomber force or, more broadly, such a massive military.

stories.headline: Ruhullah’s Real Arithmetic
stories.title: Ruhullah’s Real Arithmetic
stories.summary: Malik Daniyal’s column makes one confident claim after another about Agha Ruhullah Mehdi that he owns nothing beyond his own voice, that his Article 370 politics is a lucrative pose, that he has “never once threatened to leave” his party. Each of these claims sounds sharp on the page. None of them survives contact with the actual record. Let’s go through them one at a time. 1. His victory belonged to the party, not to him. Prove it. Daniyal states, as settled fact, that Ruhullah’s 2024 Srinagar win was built upon the National Conference’s organisational apparatus and was not a personal following assembled independently. He offers no polling data, no booth analysis, nothing. He just asserts it. Here’s what the actual numbers say. Ruhullah won Srinagar with 356,866 votes 52.85% beating Waheed Para by 188,416 votes. Compare that to 2019, when NC’s Farooq Abdullah arguably the most recognisable name in Kashmiri politics won the same seat with only 106,750 votes, on a turnout of barely 14%. In 2024, turnout rose and Ruhullah’s vote count more than tripled Farooq’s. You cannot explain that gap by pointing at the party symbol alone. Something about the candidate mattered. Daniyal never engages with this, he simply declares the conclusion he needs and moves on. And Kashmir’s own recent history undercuts the ‘voters belong to the institution’ theory anyway. In 2014, Farooq Abdullah the NC’s own patriarch lost Srinagar to PDP’s Tariq Hameed Karra. The “institution” didn’t save him that year. Voters in this city have moved between NC, PDP, independents and abstention for two decades. That’s not blind institutional loyalty. That’s an electorate making live judgments, election to election. 2. He has never threatened to leave. He had eight days before this was published. This is the essay’s most serious factual problem. Daniyal’s piece appeared on 25 August 2026 built around the idea that Ruhullah talks like a rebel but never risks anything. But on 17 August a full week earlier Ruhullah had already said, in his own words, “made up my mind” to resign from Parliament within a few months, once he had taken the fight for constitutional restoration to “a certain level.” He said this knowing exactly what it would cost him. “I won’t have the Parliament. The lobbying that I can do through the Parliament, the outreach that I can do, I won’t have that.” That is a man naming the price of his own position and saying he’ll pay it. Since then, matters have moved further, not less, in the direction that damages Daniyal’s thesis. Farooq Abdullah himself has publicly challenged Ruhullah to resign and “seek a fresh mandate” if he believes his 2024 win was personal, saying, “we will see how many votes you get.” That is the party leadership calling what it believes is a bluff the opposite of an MP quietly enjoying incumbency while talking tough. Whatever you think of how this ends, a man who has never once threatened to leave is simply not an accurate description of where things stood by publication day, and it was demonstrably inaccurate before the essay even ran. 3. “Chasing Article 370 is keeping a wound lucrative.” No it’s keeping a promise. Daniyal frames the demand for restoration as either constitutional illiteracy or a cynical grievance industry. He skips the obvious third possibility, that this was a promise the National Conference itself made to get elected and Ruhullah is one of the people who wrote it. The NC’s 2024 manifesto, its “12 guarantees” explicitly promised to “strive to restore Articles 370 and 35A and statehood as prior to August 5, 2019.” That document was drafted by senior leader Abdul Rahim Rather and by Ruhullah himself. So when Ruhullah now says the party is walking away from a commitment it sought votes on, he is not inventing a grievance to sell. He is holding his own party to a document he helped write. Calling that “keeping an old wound lucrative” only makes sense if you also believe the NC’s own manifesto was itself a cynical exercise, which is not the argument Daniyal is making but it’s the argument his logic requires. Difficulty is not the same as dishonesty. Yes the Supreme Court upheld the abrogation in 2023. Yes reversing it needs a parliamentary majority nobody currently has. That is a real obstacle. It is not proof that raising the demand is insincere, by that standard almost every hard political struggle in India from federal autonomy movements to reservation battles would have to be dismissed as fake the moment it wasn’t instantly winnable. 4. The essay talks about Ruhullah’s motives. It never once asks if he’s right. This is the real gap in “Rebel Arithmetic.” Ruhullah has made specific, checkable complaints, that he’s been excluded from internal party deliberations, that the party has “stopped striving” for the restoration it promised, that it has quietly settled for statehood alone. Daniyal repeats these charges in a line or two and then spends the rest of the essay asking whether Ruhullah is being clever, careerist or performing for a future comeback. He never asks whether Ruhullah’s actual complaint, that the party is retreating from its own manifesto is true. That is a very old trick in political commentary, when someone’s argument is inconvenient, write about their ambition instead of their argument. 5. The historical comparisons don’t do the work Daniyal needs them to do and they don’t even mean what he thinks. Yes, Ghulam Mohammad Shah, Sajad Lone, Altaf Bukhari, Imran Ansari and Muzaffar Baig all left their parties and none of them became a Valley-wide force. That’s a real pattern and it’s worth taking seriously. But look at why each of them left. They all left for a chair. Shah broke away with Delhi’s backing to grab the chief minister’s seat. Bukhari left to become a minister under an administration favourable to him. Ansari and Baig moved from party to party chasing position, cabinet berths, proximity to power. Strip away the individual details and the pattern is identical, every single name on Daniyal’s list left because he wanted office and left toward it. Power was the destination in every case. Ruhullah is the only name on this list moving in the opposite direction threatening to give up the seat he already holds, not manoeuvring for a better one, and doing it on a point of principle his own party leadership doesn’t want raised. Comparing a man risking his seat over a manifesto commitment to men who abandoned their parties chasing ministries is not a fair comparison. It’s the wrong shelf. There’s also the plain fact that every one of those cases is about a man who left. Ruhullah, as of the point Daniyal was writing, had not left and even now, any resignation he pursues would be a fresh mandate contest from his own sitting seat, not a defection to a new outfit built from scratch, which is a materially different gamble than what Shah or Bukhari attempted. Using the fate of people who exited to predict the fate of a man testing his standing through re-election is comparing two different bets. Even Sajad Lone’s case, the closest parallel Daniyal offers, cuts against him on closer look. Lone won Handwara in 2024 by only 662 votes and lost Kupwara outright. That shows how hard it is to build a durable, geographically broad organisation from nothing. It does not show that a sitting MP who has just posted an 188,000-vote margin and who is now being dared by his own party president to test that margin directly will suffer the same fate. And there is Srinagar’s own electoral memory the 2017 bypoll. This cuts even harder against the “voters belong to the institution, not the man” theory. In the 2017 Srinagar bypoll, Farooq Abdullah won with just 48,555 votes on the lowest turnout the seat has ever recorded, 7.13%, after separatists called for a boycott in the tense aftermath of the 2016 unrest and much of the electorate stayed away from the booths in protest. The seat was effectively decided by whoever could still turn out a vote in that climate and the constituency’s concentrated in Budgam and some parts of Srinagar city like Zadibal, Alamgiri Bazar etc, was the bloc that came out. Ruhullah, the most prominent political figure in central Kashmir played a central role in holding that vote for the NC that year. With most voters boycotting, it was his core constituency’s turnout that helped deliver Farooq’s winning margin. That is not a footnote. It means the party’s survival on this very seat has at least once before depended directly on Ruhullah’s own standing with a constituency the NC could not otherwise turn out. If the “institution, not the individual” theory were as absolute as Daniyal claims, that 2017 win shouldn’t have needed him at all. The real question, reversed Daniyal asks whether Ruhullah can survive without the National Conference. That’s a fair question for some future date. The more urgent one, given where things stand right now, is this; can the National Conference keep telling voters it stands for restoration of Article 370 while trying to silence the MP who co-wrote that very promise into its manifesto and is refusing to let the party quietly walk away from it? Kashmir’s political history does punish men who overestimate their own gravity Daniyal is right about that much. But the honest test of whether Ruhullah is one of them is the fresh mandate his own party president has now dared him to seek. Don’t crown him before that test. opening: Malik Daniyal’s column makes one confident claim after another about Agha Ruhullah Mehdi that he owns nothing beyond his own voice, that his Article 370 politics is a lucrative pose, that he has “never once threatened to leave” his party.
Each of these claims sounds sharp on the page.
body: None of them survives contact with the actual record.
Let’s go through them one at a time.
His victory belonged to the party, not to him.
Prove it.
Daniyal states, as settled fact, that Ruhullah’s 2024 Srinagar win was built upon the National Conference’s organisational apparatus and was not a personal following assembled independently.
He offers no polling data, no booth analysis, nothing.
He just asserts it.
Here’s what the actual numbers say.
Ruhullah won Srinagar with 356,866 votes 52.85% beating Waheed Para by 188,416 votes.
Compare that to 2019, when NC’s Farooq Abdullah arguably the most recognisable name in Kashmiri politics won the same seat with only 106,750 votes, on a turnout of barely 14%.
In 2024, turnout rose and Ruhullah’s vote count more than tripled Farooq’s.
You cannot explain that gap by pointing at the party symbol alone.
Something about the candidate mattered.
Daniyal never engages with this, he simply declares the conclusion he needs and moves on.
And Kashmir’s own recent history undercuts the ‘voters belong to the institution’ theory anyway.
In 2014, Farooq Abdullah the NC’s own patriarch lost Srinagar to PDP’s Tariq Hameed Karra.
The “institution” didn’t save him that year.
Voters in this city have moved between NC, PDP, independents and abstention for two decades.
That’s not blind institutional loyalty.
That’s an electorate making live judgments, election to election.
He has never threatened to leave.
He had eight days before this was published.
This is the essay’s most serious factual problem.
Daniyal’s piece appeared on 25 August 2026 built around the idea that Ruhullah talks like a rebel but never risks anything.

But on 17 August a full week earlier Ruhullah had already said, in his own words, “made up my mind” to resign from Parliament within a few months, once he had taken the fight for constitutional restoration to “a certain level.” He said this knowing exactly what it would cost him.
“I won’t have the Parliament.
The lobbying that I can do through the Parliament, the outreach that I can do, I won’t have that.” That is a man naming the price of his own position and saying he’ll pay it.
Since then, matters have moved further, not less, in the direction that damages Daniyal’s thesis.

Farooq Abdullah himself has publicly challenged Ruhullah to resign and “seek a fresh mandate” if he believes his 2024 win was personal, saying, “we will see how many votes you get.” That is the party leadership calling what it believes is a bluff the opposite of an MP quietly enjoying incumbency while talking tough.

Whatever you think of how this ends, a man who has never once threatened to leave is simply not an accurate description of where things stood by publication day, and it was demonstrably inaccurate before the essay even ran.
“Chasing Article 370 is keeping a wound lucrative.” No it’s keeping a promise.
Daniyal frames the demand for restoration as either constitutional illiteracy or a cynical grievance industry.
He skips the obvious third possibility, that this was a promise the National Conference itself made to get elected and Ruhullah is one of the people who wrote it.

The NC’s 2024 manifesto, its “12 guarantees” explicitly promised to “strive to restore Articles 370 and 35A and statehood as prior to August 5, 2019.” That document was drafted by senior leader Abdul Rahim Rather and by Ruhullah himself.
So when Ruhullah now says the party is walking away from a commitment it sought votes on, he is not inventing a grievance to sell.
He is holding his own party to a document he helped write.

Calling that “keeping an old wound lucrative” only makes sense if you also believe the NC’s own manifesto was itself a cynical exercise, which is not the argument Daniyal is making but it’s the argument his logic requires.
Difficulty is not the same as dishonesty.
Yes the Supreme Court upheld the abrogation in 2023.
Yes reversing it needs a parliamentary majority nobody currently has.
That is a real obstacle.

It is not proof that raising the demand is insincere, by that standard almost every hard political struggle in India from federal autonomy movements to reservation battles would have to be dismissed as fake the moment it wasn’t instantly winnable.
The essay talks about Ruhullah’s motives.
It never once asks if he’s right.

This is the real gap in “Rebel Arithmetic.” Ruhullah has made specific, checkable complaints, that he’s been excluded from internal party deliberations, that the party has “stopped striving” for the restoration it promised, that it has quietly settled for statehood alone.
Daniyal repeats these charges in a line or two and then spends the rest of the essay asking whether Ruhullah is being clever, careerist or performing for a future comeback.
He never asks whether Ruhullah’s actual complaint, that the party is retreating from its own manifesto is true.
That is a very old trick in political commentary, when someone’s argument is inconvenient, write about their ambition instead of their argument.
The historical comparisons don’t do the work Daniyal needs them to do and they don’t even mean what he thinks.
Yes, Ghulam Mohammad Shah, Sajad Lone, Altaf Bukhari, Imran Ansari and Muzaffar Baig all left their parties and none of them became a Valley-wide force.
That’s a real pattern and it’s worth taking seriously.
But look at why each of them left.
They all left for a chair.
Shah broke away with Delhi’s backing to grab the chief minister’s seat.
Bukhari left to become a minister under an administration favourable to him.
Ansari and Baig moved from party to party chasing position, cabinet berths, proximity to power.
Strip away the individual details and the pattern is identical, every single name on Daniyal’s list left because he wanted office and left toward it.
Power was the destination in every case.

Ruhullah is the only name on this list moving in the opposite direction threatening to give up the seat he already holds, not manoeuvring for a better one, and doing it on a point of principle his own party leadership doesn’t want raised.
Comparing a man risking his seat over a manifesto commitment to men who abandoned their parties chasing ministries is not a fair comparison.
It’s the wrong shelf.
There’s also the plain fact that every one of those cases is about a man who left.

Ruhullah, as of the point Daniyal was writing, had not left and even now, any resignation he pursues would be a fresh mandate contest from his own sitting seat, not a defection to a new outfit built from scratch, which is a materially different gamble than what Shah or Bukhari attempted.
Using the fate of people who exited to predict the fate of a man testing his standing through re-election is comparing two different bets.
Even Sajad Lone’s case, the closest parallel Daniyal offers, cuts against him on closer look.
Lone won Handwara in 2024 by only 662 votes and lost Kupwara outright.
That shows how hard it is to build a durable, geographically broad organisation from nothing.
It does not show that a sitting MP who has just posted an 188,000-vote margin and who is now being dared by his own party president to test that margin directly will suffer the same fate.
And there is Srinagar’s own electoral memory the 2017 bypoll.
This cuts even harder against the “voters belong to the institution, not the man” theory.

The seat was effectively decided by whoever could still turn out a vote in that climate and the constituency’s concentrated in Budgam and some parts of Srinagar city like Zadibal, Alamgiri Bazar etc, was the bloc that came out.
Ruhullah, the most prominent political figure in central Kashmir played a central role in holding that vote for the NC that year.
With most voters boycotting, it was his core constituency’s turnout that helped deliver Farooq’s winning margin.
That is not a footnote.
It means the party’s survival on this very seat has at least once before depended directly on Ruhullah’s own standing with a constituency the NC could not otherwise turn out.
If the “institution, not the individual” theory were as absolute as Daniyal claims, that 2017 win shouldn’t have needed him at all.
The real question, reversed Daniyal asks whether Ruhullah can survive without the National Conference.
That’s a fair question for some future date.

The more urgent one, given where things stand right now, is this; can the National Conference keep telling voters it stands for restoration of Article 370 while trying to silence the MP who co-wrote that very promise into its manifesto and is refusing to let the party quietly walk away from it?
Kashmir’s political history does punish men who overestimate their own gravity Daniyal is right about that much.
But the honest test of whether Ruhullah is one of them is the fresh mandate his own party president has now dared him to seek.
Don’t crown him before that test.
But don’t bury him with an essay built on a threat to leave that had already been made, and a motive-question that avoids the substance of what he’s actually saying.

stories.title: Understanding tariff, and the hike
stories.summary: The recent power tariff hike in Jammu and Kashmir has created quite a fierce debate on the social media and amongst the society. Many statistics were tossed around in news reports about the hike in different categories of consumers, the cost of purchase of energy and the recovery thereof. The standard practice across the country is to determine the tariff every year. In case of J&K it was last done in 2023 and hence was overdue. As a matter of fact, this exercise should have been completed before the start of the financial year i.e., latest by end of March. It is now being done after five months into the current financial year. As per the Electricity Act of 2003, electricity tariff is determined by the appropriate electricity regulatory commission. For state distribution utilities (like JPDCL and KPDCL), the State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC) decides retail supply tariffs for consumers within the state. Prior to reorganisation of the State in 2019, Jammu & Kashmir had its State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC) which determined the tariff. After the reorganisation SERC was replaced by Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission (JERC). The operating principles of the Commission, however, remain the same i.e., to determine tariff in a transparent way while being guided by the need to ensure efficiency, protect consumer interests, and progressively reduce cross-subsidies while moving toward the actual cost of supply. The tariff policy under the Act also requires a fair, open, and transparent process for all parts of the electricity sector i.e., generation, transmission, and distribution. The Commission determines the tariff through a cost-based approach, where the regulator examines expenses such as power purchase cost, operation and maintenance, capital cost, return on equity, and other approved costs. The process involves submission of a petition by the utility (JPDCL or KPDCL in our case) to JERC in which it submits its accounts as regards the purchase of energy, the losses, the cost of distributing it to consumers. The JERC is expected to check these in detail and satisfy themselves to their correctness. Once found in order the expense is allowed – in case the expense is not admissible or it is more than the standard norm the Regulator can allow part, or completely disallow the expense. If the State Government wants to keep consumer tariffs below the level fixed by the Commission, it can provide a subsidy in advance through its budget provision. This means the legal tariff can remain cost-reflective while selected consumer groups receive relief through government support. The case in point is the often discussed 200 units of free power. While the utility will submit its petition and the Regulator will fix the tariff, the government can decide to foot the bill for 200 units of the consumers at the rate determined by JERC. This way there is no adverse impact on the financial health of the utility (JPDCL or KPDCL). The utilities (JPDCL or KPDCL) estimate the cost of purchasing and distributing the energy and these calculations are to be checked and verified by the Regulator who then accordingly determines the tariff to be paid by the consumers. Prior to unbundling of the power sector, which led to creation of the utilities, the Power Development Department worked out the costings and petitioned the Regulator for determination of tariff. The utilities are commercial entities who are mandated to provide energy to the consumers in an efficient and competitive manner. It is worth mentioning here that the electricity tariff in J&K is amongst the lowest in the country. Based on existing tariff structure our average domestic tariff is Rs 3.90 per unit while the two states having tariff lower than us were Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, both with average domestic tariff marginally lower at Rs 3.80 per unit. States like Maharashtra and West Bengal have an average domestic tariff of Rs 8.20 and Rs 7.40 per unit. Incidentally, J&K had the highest ‘T&D Losses’ in the country. In the year 2023-24 J&K’s losses stood at 48% followed by Arunachal Pradesh at 34% while the All India average was well below 20%. In the last few years these losses have been now substantially reduced are somewhere between 35 to 40%. This is a huge achievement and with the efforts of the utilities and cooperation of the consumers it should be possible to bring the figure down to the national average of around 15%. With the reduction in the T&D losses the tariff will also stabilise and the subsidy component currently funded by the UT Government will be used towards funding other welfare schemes. Equally, the other big achievement is the installation of pre-paid meters. The pre-paid concept itself is so alien to most of us particularly when it had been ingrained in us that electricity should be supplied free of cost. Though there is still a lot of work to do on that front commendable strides have been made in this important area. Without the cooperation of the consumers neither of these two achievements would have been possible. Frankly, a few years back nobody could have thought that such reduction in the losses and on installation of meters was achievable in such a short duration. Both the initiatives needed a complete change of mindset to be successful. Now looking at the financials projected in the tariff petition for the year 2026-2027 the projected cost of purchase and distribution of electricity for the two utilities i.e., JPDCL and KPDCL, is Rs 10276 crores. Out of this, Rs 7856 crores are expected to be collected leaving a shortfall in revenue collection of Rs 2421 crores. This amount of Rs 2421 crores is being funded by the government and will not be passed on to the consumers. Since an amount of Rs 502 crores is expected to be collected by increasing the tariff it implies that the actual shortfall in revenue collection, without increase in tariff would have been Rs 2923 crores. While a figure of 6.83% increase in tariff has been mentioned, this figure for consumers other than domestic, is much higher. Only in case of the BPL consumers it is unchanged at Rs 1.40 per unit subject to a maximum of 30 units per month. A preliminary review of the 334-page order issued by the JERC throws up a number of questions that demand clarification: i. If both JPDCL and KPDCL in their tariff petitions had asked for only a 5% across-the-board increase why did JERC approve a much higher tariff structure across different categories of consumers? What is the rationale behind this additional increase? ii. As per the Order the current hike will be effective 1 Sep 26 and will be valid till 31 Mar 27. What happens after Mar 2027? iii. Since the cost of purchase and distribution of electricity is for the full financial year (26-27) and the new tariff regime will be implemented only from 1 Sep 26, how will the full amount of Rs 502 crores be collected by billing at revised tariff for only 7 months (Sep 26 to Mar 27) instead of estimated 12 months in the petition? iv. The Order has considered Time of Day tariff. While it will have an impact the billing for domestic consumers during the peak hours because of 10% surcharge, it will positively effect the commercial and industrial consumers during the solar hours. Most of the commercial establishments and industries operate during the day and thus their bills for solar hour consumption will be reduced by 20% because of the rebate on ToD tariff. The impact of the rebate and of surcharge has not been captured in the calculations. v. The Order has not considered the impact of roof top solar units. Because of the generation from these roof top solar installations there will be lesser withdrawal of energy from the system and thence lesser purchase of energy from grid. Even though the installed capacity is small, it is only proper to capture its impact in the Order. For the hearing on KPDCL petition there hasn’t been much of a public consultation and participation. Only three stakeholders attended the hearing of KPDCL and as can be seen from the Order they did not engage in any interaction during the hearing nor had they submitted any objections against the KPDCL petition. However, in the hearing held in Jammu for the JPDCL petition there were 32 stakeholders / consumers present in the hearing and a total of 13 objections were submitted against the proposed hike of 5% in the JPDCL petition. Going forward, for utilities to win the confidence of consumers, it is time to invest in transparent public outreach and shift toward a partnership-based approach. Engaging stakeholders is not optional; continuous engagement with stakeholders is critical to ensuring that the public not only understands but also supports the initiatives and programmes launched by the utilities. Iftikhar A Drabu is a Civil Engineer

stories.headline: Birdi passes the baton, Kumar takes charge
stories.title: Birdi passes the baton, Kumar takes charge
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 27: Senior IPS officer Sujit Kumar on Thursday evening took over as Inspector General of Police (IGP), Kashmir Zone, after the Jammu and Kashmir Home Department transferred him from IGP Security, J&K, as part of a 14-officer police reshuffle ordered with immediate effect. Kumar, a 2007-batch officer of the AGMUT cadre, has been posted as IG Kashmir Zone against an available vacancy, succeeding Vidhi Kumar Birdi, who headed the Kashmir police establishment and also held additional charge of IGP Armed Police Kashmir. Birdi, a 2003-batch officer, had earlier been cleared for central deputation as Inspector General in the CRPF; his relieving had been held back during the Amarnath Ji Yatra and is now linked to the vacancy at the Kashmir Zone. The takeover places Kumar at the head of the Valley police force at a time when the security grid remains focused on counter-terror operations, intelligence coordination, protection of vital installations and close working with the Army and Central Armed Police Forces. Kumar assumed the new charge after more than two years as IGP Security J&K, a posting he held from August 2024 following his functional promotion to the IGP rank. In that role he oversaw the security architecture for protected persons and key installations. Earlier this month, Security Headquarters granted in-situ promotion to 1,028 personnel of different ranks under a process chaired by him. His field record in the Union Territory includes DIG North Kashmir, DIG Central Kashmir with additional charge of South Kashmir, DIG CID Kashmir, DIG Udhampur-Reasi Range and DIG Jammu-Kathua-Samba Range. He has also served in Ladakh during his career. In March 2025 the Ministry of Home Affairs approved his deputation as DIG in the CRPF for five years, but he was not relieved and continued in J&K.

stories.title: M K Sinha is new CID chief, Sujit Kumar is IGP Kashmir
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 27: The Jammu and Kashmir government on Thursday ordered a major reshuffle in the police administration, appointing senior IPS officer M K Sinha as the new Additional Director General of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID), J&K, while Sujit Kumar has been posted as Inspector General of Police (IGP), Kashmir Zone, as part of a wider transfer and posting of 14 senior IPS and JKPS officers. The changes are part of a wider reshuffle involving 14 senior IPS and JKPS officers and were ordered with immediate effect by the Home Department under Government Order Non438-Home of 2026, dated August 27. M K Sinha, an IPS officer of the 1996 AGMUT cadre, has been shifted from his present position as ADG Headquarters and posted as ADG CID J&K, replacing Nitish Kumar. Nitish Kumar, IPS (AGMUT:1999), has been transferred from CID and posted as ADG Armed Police J&K against an available vacancy. The government has also made a key change in the Kashmir Zone, with Sujit Kumar, IPS (AGMUT:2007), appointed as IGP Kashmir Zone. Kumar, who was serving as IG Security, has been moved to the Kashmir Zone against an available vacancy. His transfer also triggered a change in the Security Wing, with Vivek Gupta, IPS (AGMUT:2007), appointed as IGP Security, replacing Sujit Kumar. stories.headline: Kashmir summer to end with brief late-August heat
stories.title: Kashmir summer to end with brief late-August heat
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 27: Kashmir's summer is set to end with a brief heat spell, as the Meteorological (MeT) Department forecasts temperatures to rise toward 35 degrees Celsius in the Valley plains over the next few days. Friday and Saturday are expected to be the hottest days. Srinagar recorded 32.9 degrees Celsius on Thursday. Kupwara recorded 33.3 degrees Celsius and Qazigund 32 degrees Celsius. Kokernag recorded 31.7 degrees Celsius, Pahalgam 27 degrees Celsius and Gulmarg 24 degrees Celsius. Jammu city recorded 35 degrees Celsius and Katra 32.7 degrees Celsius. Banihal recorded 30.1 degrees Celsius, Bhaderwah 30.2 degrees Celsius, and Batote 28 degrees Celsius. The MeT has forecast dry and warmer weather through the end of August, mainly in the plains with showers at isolated places. Higher reaches are likely to remain cooler. A moderate summer May was cooler, with temperatures mostly in the 20s and occasional days touching 30s. The plains received mostly light to moderate rain, while higher reaches experienced frequent and intense, localised showers. Some spells were more widespread, while isolated areas also reported hailstorms. June and July remained moderate overall. Cloud cover, rain, and wet spells kept temperatures in check, although both months saw brief heat spells. However, the month of June ended with a brief heat spell lasting a few days. Srinagar touched 35.3 degrees Celsius on June 29 and 35.5 degrees Celsius on June 30. July began relatively cool before a brief mid-month heat spell pushed Srinagar to 35 degrees Celsius on July 17 and 35.9 degrees Celsius on July 18, the season's highest so far. Temperatures eased afterward, with another short warm spell toward the end of July. Rainfall during June and July was mostly localized, though some spells were widespread. Intense showers also caused hailstorms, landslides, mudslides and flash floods in parts of the Valley and Jammu. August stayed moderate August was mostly dry, but temperatures remained moderate, generally around 30-32 degrees Celsius in the Valley plains. Rainfall was largely confined to isolated, intense showers in higher reaches and brief light to moderate spells in the plains. The late-August rise in temperatures is expected to be brief. Cooler than 2025 The contrast with last summer is marked, as Kashmir witnessed prolonged heat spells in June and July. Srinagar recorded 37.2 degrees Celsius on July 6, 2025, and 36.2 degrees Celsius on July 29. June 2025 was the hottest June in Srinagar since 1978. The city recorded an average maximum of about 33 degrees Celsius, nearly three degrees above normal. For 10 consecutive days, temperatures crossed 34 degrees Celsius. A prolonged dry spell and about 50 percent rainfall deficit contributed to the heat. Even consecutive wet spells in late July and August did little to end the heat. Conditions remained largely hot and humid. This summer, wet spells during May, June and July repeatedly checked temperatures. Heat spells were brief, while August remained moderate despite mostly dry weather. Srinagar's seasonal high of 35.9 degrees Celsius was 1.3 degrees below last year's 37.2 degrees Celsius peak. Summer gives way to autumn June, July, and August mark Kashmir's summer period. With August ending, the Valley is entering its seasonal transition. Warm afternoons can persist through September, even as nights gradually become cooler. The transition becomes more noticeable after September 21, with warmer days and cooler nights signalling the approach of autumn. The shift strengthens through October as temperatures decline. For now, Kashmir is set for one final late-summer heat spell after a significantly milder summer than 2025.
